     EXHIBIT K
DEVIATION REQUEST
4/5/2022

Draper City Planning Commission
1020 E. Pioneer Rd.
Draper, UT 84020

Re: Trailside Townhomes Multi-Family Dwelling Development Standards Deviations

Dear Planning Commission:

Ikon Development (Ikon) has submitted for site plan approval a 152-unit townhome development at the intersection of Brookings Dr. and
Maple Bluff Rd. This development meets or exceeds the multi-family dwelling development standards set forth in the Draper City Code of
Ordinances except for two following deviations:

    1.     Ikon hereby requests a deviation from the standards in section 9-32-030-B3 requiring 50% brick, stone, or synthetic stone
    2.     Ikon also requests a deviation from the standards in section 9-32-030-D4 calling for sidewalks on both sides of the private streets.

Exterior Material Deviation

The Trailside Townhomes (Trailside) development falls under the purview of Section 9-32-030-B3 of the Multi-Family Dwelling Development
Standards, which state that, “Building materials for multiple-family structures shall consist of at least fifty percent (50%) brick, stone, or
synthetic stone on all sides of the structure.” This section goes on to list two specific instances where the Planning Commission may grant a
deviation from these requirements. The latter of these two requirements states the following:

    •    “If a predominant building material exists in the project vicinity and the use of the material will uphold the existing character and
         style of the given neighborhood.”

To satisfy this deviation, the current design uses a series of high-quality, primary materials – fiber cement siding and stone – as defined in
the Chapter 22 Design Standards and Guidelines. While Chapter 22 governs commercial, public, and industrial projects, the definition of
high-quality, primary materials is still relevant and applicable.

Ikon understands the purpose of standards is to encourage the use of these high-quality materials and architecture in the construction of
multi-family structures. Taken together as a whole, the DOT-Architecture and Ikon teams believe that the proposed materials, will be
applied in such a way to create 360° architecture and to form a pleasing, modern mountain aesthetic. The Trailside development builds on
the existing mountain-style design aesthetic of the residential developments along and around Suncrest Dr. and Traverse Ridge Rd. The
proposed development further refines the aesthetic by replacing minimal front faux stone and stucco remainder widely used in the nearby
single-family neighborhood with following upscale materials:

    1.   The stone finish – The Monument stone finish from Eldorado Stone’s SierraCut24 collection or a similar stone, brick or stone
         veneer wraps the entirety of the first floor on each building, anchoring the townhomes with a solid base.
    2.   The fiber cement siding – Hardie plank lap siding and Hardie shingle siding – is the primary façade material on the upper floors,
         providing an opportunity to add color to each building, which contributes to the 360° architecture, while also helping with
         wayfinding.

The submitted material board sheet (A200), sample elevations showing the common building types (A201 & A211), and exterior rendering
(A901) visually show the elements that are outlined above.

Looking beyond the immediate area, we have surveyed multi-family structures in Draper City that are under construction or have been
recently completed. Many buildings may have received deviations or have an overall aesthetic established in a special district that appear
not to meet the 50% brick or stone standard. These buildings still present an upscale look that exudes a quality ambiance without arbitrary
application of brick or stone materials. Other observed buildings seem to strictly meet the 50% standard but have brick and stone
applications that stop midway on an architectural element in an artificial way that does not achieve the desired quality look.

In analyzing the Trailside project look against the current practical application of brick and stone standard in the area and Draper City, it
makes sense that Trailside has a stone underpinning on the first floor that architecturally anchors the structure, serves the purpose of
protecting the building where soil or snow may have prolonged contact with the building and provides a pleasing appearance where
residents have immediate interaction with the exterior materials. The resulting mountain style architecture takes some key elements of the
“Swiss Chalet” form of a stone base and upper floor wood exterior with balconies to create a modern vernacular or interpretation of this
time-honored mountain architectural tradition. Ikon does not feel that adding additional stone to the upper portions of the elevations
would enhance the architecture but could detract from the desired appearance.

Sidewalk Deviation

This Trailside development also falls under the scope of Section 9-32-030-D4 of the Multi-family Dwelling Development Standards, which
state that “Multiple-family projects shall install sidewalks on both sides of all private streets.” This section goes on to list specific instances
where the Planning Commission may grant a deviation from these requirements as follows:

    •    “The planning commission may permit a deviation from the requirement for sidewalks on both sides of a private street by
         eliminating the sidewalk or a portion of the sidewalk on one side of the street upon finding all of the following:
             o The second sidewalk or portion of the sidewalk does not provide pedestrian connectivity to any units or amenities;
             o Ample pedestrian circulation has been provided;
             o The purpose and intent of the development standards set forth in this chapter are met; and
             o The second sidewalk or portion thereof is unnecessary and/or undesirable.”

Ikon recognizes the importance of having connectivity throughout the Trailside development for both convenience and safety. This is a
guiding principle in the project design in conjunction with the following additional design goals:

    1.   Ikon seeks to maximize the previously Draper City approved density of 160 units while minimizing the impact on the natural sloped
         hillsides surrounding the buildable areas of the site.
    2.   Ikon wishes to create a mountain side natural ambiance complementary to the design guidelines of the Suncrest development
         standards by eliminating unnecessary or undesirable hardscape or sidewalks.

To achieve these design goals the Ikon design team has incorporated the following design principles into creating the project:

Mountain Ambiance

The Suncrest development resides in a setting blessed with mountain views and a beautiful natural setting that coexists with urban
development. To lessen the impact on the natural setting, Suncrest has adopted master planning guidelines that have reduced right-of-way
and dictate less hardscape. Although Trailside Townhomes falls under the authority of the Draper City multiple family dwelling standards,
we have sought to inculcate this same mountain ambiance into our project by reducing hardscape in our walkways. Thus, sidewalk has been
eliminated from one side of the right-of-way while still having ample pedestrian access to each portion of the development. To further
create a trail like ambiance we will be posting a speed limit of fifteen miles per hour. Having less hardscape and a lower speed limit will
create a neighborhood feeling that encourages resident interaction.

Slope Friendly Design

Significant areas that border the most buildable portion of site are steep uphill and downhill slopes. To lessen impact on these slopes,
wider, but less deep fronted loaded units that minimized slope encroachment were designed for selected areas of the site. This is
particularly critical for the units located on the narrow western section of site where the slopes are particularly steep, but that has less
traffic as only thirty units are placed in that six plus acres of the site. By having front loaded units, most walkways are eliminated in the rear
of buildings where slope impact would be the greatest. To enhance circulation beyond the single sidewalk in this narrow western area of
the site, an east-west trail was added to provide additional connectivity to the western units and to the amenities of a sun deck and dog
park.

In the central and eastern third of the site where most buildable area exists, narrow, but deeper units with rear loaded entries were
designed so the allotted density could be largely achieved. Most central or eastern units have both sidewalks at the driveways and rear
walks that connect to each entry door. Some units in the middle area that have only rear entries on a pedestrian friendly courtyard as the
sidewalks on the front of the units were unnecessary to provide ample pedestrian circulation.

Using these methodologies, we have almost achieved the allotted density with 152 proposed units out of the 160-unit allotment. By using
single sidewalks on most streets, great connectivity to the units and the various common amenities of gathering decks, the dog park, pool
area and pickleball courts has been preserved without sacrificing the desired mountain side ambiance and neighborhood friendly feeling.

Thank you,



James Wheatley
